claim: TCF/LEF factors are ancient context-dependent enhancer-binding proteins that are activated by β-catenin following Wnt signaling.
source: TCF/LEF factors are ancient context-dependent enhancer-binding proteins that are activated by β-catenin following Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: TCF/LEF factors control embryonic development and adult stem cell compartments.
source: They control embryonic development and adult stem cell compartments, and their dysregulation often causes cancer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references in the introduction.

claim: Dysregulation of TCF/LEF factors often causes cancer.
source: They control embryonic development and adult stem cell compartments, and their dysregulation often causes cancer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and discussed in the context of cancer in the discussion section.

claim: β-catenin-dependent transcription relies on the NPF motif of Pygo proteins.
source: β-catenin-dependent transcription relies on the NPF motif of Pygo proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Chip/LDB-SSDP (ChiLS) complex is the ligand specifically binding to NPF.
source: Here, we use a proteomics approach to discover the Chip/LDB-SSDP (ChiLS) complex as the ligand specifically binding to NPF.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 2A and co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 2B-D.

claim: ChiLS recognizes NPF motifs in Runt/RUNX2.
source: ChiLS also recognizes NPF motifs in other nuclear factors including Runt/RUNX2 and Drosophila ARID1, and binds to Groucho/TLE.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by NMR binding assays in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ChiLS recognizes NPF motifs in Drosophila ARID1.
source: ChiLS also recognizes NPF motifs in other nuclear factors including Runt/RUNX2 and Drosophila ARID1, and binds to Groucho/TLE.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by NMR binding assays in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: ChiLS binds to Groucho/TLE.
source: ChiLS also recognizes NPF motifs in other nuclear factors including Runt/RUNX2 and Drosophila ARID1, and binds to Groucho/TLE.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by mass spectrometry (Figure 7A) and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 7B-D).

claim: ChiLS confers context-dependence on TCF/LEF by integrating multiple inputs from lineage and signal-responsive factors.
source: Together with previous evidence, our study indicates that ChiLS confers context-dependence on TCF/LEF by integrating multiple inputs from lineage and signal-responsive factors, including enhanceosome switch-off by Notch.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by the functional analysis of Drosophila midgut enhancers and discussion of ChiLS interactions.

claim: ChiLS mediates enhanceosome switch-off by Notch.
source: Together with previous evidence, our study indicates that ChiLS confers context-dependence on TCF/LEF by integrating multiple inputs from lineage and signal-responsive factors, including enhanceosome switch-off by Notch.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and discussed in the context of enhanceosome switching in the discussion section.

claim: The integrity of ChiLS is crucial in the avoidance of cancer due to its pivotal function in embryos and stem cells.
source: Its pivotal function in embryos and stem cells explain why its integrity is crucial in the avoidance of cancer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and discussed in the 'Links to human cancer' section of the discussion.

claim: TCF/LEF factors were discovered as context-dependent architectural factors without intrinsic transactivation potential that bind to the T cell receptor α (TCRα) enhancer via their high mobility group (HMG) domain.
source: TCF/LEF factors (TCFs) were discovered as context-dependent architectural factors without intrinsic transactivation potential that bind to the T cell receptor α (TCRα) enhancer via their high mobility group (HMG) domain (Waterman and Jones, 1990; Giese et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to original discovery papers.

claim: TCF/LEF factors facilitate complex assemblies with other nearby enhancer-binding proteins, including CREB and RUNX1.
source: They facilitate complex assemblies with other nearby enhancer-binding proteins, including the signal-responsive CRE-binding factor (CREB) and the lineage-specific RUNX1 (also called Acute Myeloid Leukemia 1, AML1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the analysis of the TCRα enhancer.

claim: TCF activity depends on β-catenin, a transcriptional co-factor activated by Wnt signaling.
source: Their activity further depends on β-catenin, a transcriptional co-factor activated by Wnt signaling, an ancient signaling pathway that controls animal development and stem cell compartments, and whose dysregulation often causes cancer (Clevers, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Wnt signaling is an ancient signaling pathway that controls animal development and stem cell compartments.
source: Their activity further depends on β-catenin, a transcriptional co-factor activated by Wnt signaling, an ancient signaling pathway that controls animal development and stem cell compartments, and whose dysregulation often causes cancer (Clevers, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Dysregulation of Wnt signaling often causes cancer.
source: Their activity further depends on β-catenin, a transcriptional co-factor activated by Wnt signaling, an ancient signaling pathway that controls animal development and stem cell compartments, and whose dysregulation often causes cancer (Clevers, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: dTCF integrates multiple signaling inputs with lineage-specific cues during endoderm induction in the embryonic midgut of Drosophila.
source: The context-dependence of TCFs is also apparent in other systems, for example in the embryonic midgut of Drosophila where dTCF integrates multiple signaling inputs with lineage-specific cues during endoderm induction (Riese et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: In the absence of signaling, TCFs are bound by Groucho/TLE proteins.
source: In the absence of signaling, T cell factors (TCFs) are bound by the Groucho/Transducin-like Enhancer-of-split (Groucho/TLE) proteins, a family of co-repressors that silence TCF enhancers by recruiting histone deacetylases (HDACs) (Turki-Judeh and Courey, 2012) and by 'blanketing' them with inactive chromatin (Sekiya and Zaret, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Groucho/TLE proteins silence TCF enhancers by recruiting histone deacetylases (HDACs).
source: In the absence of signaling, T cell factors (TCFs) are bound by the Groucho/Transducin-like Enhancer-of-split (Groucho/TLE) proteins, a family of co-repressors that silence TCF enhancers by recruiting histone deacetylases (HDACs) (Turki-Judeh and Courey, 2012) and by 'blanketing' them with inactive chromatin (Sekiya and Zaret, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Groucho/TLE proteins silence TCF enhancers by 'blanketing' them with inactive chromatin.
source: In the absence of signaling, T cell factors (TCFs) are bound by the Groucho/Transducin-like Enhancer-of-split (Groucho/TLE) proteins, a family of co-repressors that silence TCF enhancers by recruiting histone deacetylases (HDACs) (Turki-Judeh and Courey, 2012) and by 'blanketing' them with inactive chromatin (Sekiya and Zaret, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: TLEs are displaced from TCFs by β-catenin following Wnt signaling.
source: TLEs are displaced from TCFs by β-catenin following Wnt signaling, however this is not achieved by competitive binding (Chodaparambil et al., 2014) but depends on other factors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Displacement of TLEs from TCFs by β-catenin is not achieved by competitive binding.
source: TLEs are displaced from TCFs by β-catenin following Wnt signaling, however this is not achieved by competitive binding (Chodaparambil et al., 2014) but depends on other factors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Pygopus (Pygo) is a conserved nuclear Wnt signaling factor that recruits Armadillo via the Legless/BCL9 adaptor to promote TCF-dependent transcription.
source: One of these is Pygopus (Pygo), a conserved nuclear Wnt signaling factor that recruits Armadillo (Drosophila β-catenin) via the Legless/BCL9 adaptor to promote TCF-dependent transcription (Kramps et al., 2002; Parker et al., 2002; Thompson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Pygo is largely dispensable in the absence of Groucho.
source: Intriguingly, Pygo is largely dispensable in the absence of Groucho (Mieszczanek et al., 2008), which implicates this protein in alleviating Groucho-dependent repression of Wg targets.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Pygo is implicated in alleviating Groucho-dependent repression of Wg targets.
source: Intriguingly, Pygo is largely dispensable in the absence of Groucho (Mieszczanek et al., 2008), which implicates this protein in alleviating Groucho-dependent repression of Wg targets.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation and is an inference from the genetic data.

claim: Pygo has a C-terminal plant homology domain (PHD) and an N-terminal asparagine proline phenylalanine (NPF) motif, each essential for development and tissue patterning.
source: Pygo has a C-terminal plant homology domain (PHD) and an N-terminal asparagine proline phenylalanine (NPF) motif, each essential for development and tissue patterning (Mosimann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: The Pygo PHD finger binds to Legless/BCL9.
source: Much is known about the PHD finger, which binds to Legless/BCL9 (Kramps et al., 2002) and to histone H3 tail methylated at lysine 4 via opposite surfaces (Fiedler et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2013) that are connected by allosteric communication (Miller et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The Pygo PHD finger binds to histone H3 tail methylated at lysine 4.
source: Much is known about the PHD finger, which binds to Legless/BCL9 (Kramps et al., 2002) and to histone H3 tail methylated at lysine 4 via opposite surfaces (Fiedler et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2013) that are connected by allosteric communication (Miller et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The Legless/BCL9 and histone H3 binding surfaces of the Pygo PHD finger are connected by allosteric communication.
source: Much is known about the PHD finger, which binds to Legless/BCL9 (Kramps et al., 2002) and to histone H3 tail methylated at lysine 4 via opposite surfaces (Fiedler et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2013) that are connected by allosteric communication (Miller et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Chip, SSDP and three LIM domain proteins (Beadex, CG5708, and Apterous) were discovered amongst the top hits specifically associated with wild-type but not mutant Pygo.
source: We thus discovered Chip, SSDP and three LIM domain proteins—Beadex and CG5708 (both LIM-only proteins, LMO) and Apterous (an LHX)—amongst the top hits specifically associated with wt but not mutant Pygo (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Chip dimerizes through DD (dimerization domain).
source: These proteins are known to form a complex: Chip dimerizes through DD (dimerization domain) and binds to SSDP through LDB/Chip conserved domain (LCCD) and to LIM domains through LIM-interacting domain (LID).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is based on known structural information.

claim: Chip binds to SSDP through LCCD (LDB/Chip conserved domain).
source: These proteins are known to form a complex: Chip dimerizes through DD (dimerization domain) and binds to SSDP through LDB/Chip conserved domain (LCCD) and to LIM domains through LIM-interacting domain (LID).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is based on known structural information.

claim: Chip binds to LIM domains through LID (LIM-interacting domain).
source: These proteins are known to form a complex: Chip dimerizes through DD (dimerization domain) and binds to SSDP through LDB/Chip conserved domain (LCCD) and to LIM domains through LIM-interacting domain (LID).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is based on known structural information.

claim: ChiLS associates with enhancers directly through LHX (e.g., Apterous) or indirectly through LMO adaptors that bind to bHLH and GATA factors.
source: The latter allow ChiLS to associate with enhancers, either directly through LHX (e.g., Apterous), or indirectly through LMO adaptors that bind to bHLH (e.g., Achaete/Scute) and GATA factors (e.g., Pannier) (Bronstein and Segal, 2011; Love et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations.

claim: LMOs displace LHXs from ChiLS by virtue of their high expression level and/or high affinity for LID.
source: Indeed, LMOs displace LHXs from ChiLS by virtue of their high expression level and/or high affinity for LID (Milan and Cohen, 1999; Ramain et al., 2000; Matthews et al., 2008), and are thus capable of switching from LHX to GATA/bHLH.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations.

claim: ChiLS components were found associated with Pygo2 in stably transfected HEK293T cell lines.
source: We also found ChiLS components associated with Pygo2 in stably transfected HEK293T cell lines, and with recombinant triple-NPF baits in lysates from mouse brains and colorectal cancer cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: ChiLS components were found associated with recombinant triple-NPF baits in lysates from mouse brains and colorectal cancer cell lines.
source: We also found ChiLS components associated with Pygo2 in stably transfected HEK293T cell lines, and with recombinant triple-NPF baits in lysates from mouse brains and colorectal cancer cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Wild-type but not NPF-mutant HA-Pygo2 coIPs with endogenous LDB1.
source: Furthermore, wt but not mutant HA-Pygo2 coIPs with endogenous LDB1, and vice versa (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The conserved proline cluster upstream of NPF is required for binding to LDB1.
source: The conserved proline cluster upstream of NPF is also required for binding, consistent with transcription assays in S2 cells that indicated the function of this cluster (Stadeli and Basler, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data and a citation.

claim: LID is dispensable for LDB1 binding to Pygo2.
source: Testing truncations of LDB1 for coIP with Pygo2, we found that LID is dispensable for binding, whereas dimerization seems important since there is little interaction with Pygo2 in the absence of DD (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Dimerization is important for LDB1 binding to Pygo2.
source: Testing truncations of LDB1 for coIP with Pygo2, we found that LID is dispensable for binding, whereas dimerization seems important since there is little interaction with Pygo2 in the absence of DD (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: LDB1 coIPs with Pygo2 in a dose-dependent way upon co-expression.
source: Importantly, LDB1 coIPs with Pygo2 in a dose-dependent way upon co-expression, whereas SSDP hardly coIPs with Pygo2 in the absence of exogenous LDB1, even at high SSDP excess (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SSDP hardly coIPs with Pygo2 in the absence of exogenous LDB1, even at high SSDP excess.
source: Importantly, LDB1 coIPs with Pygo2 in a dose-dependent way upon co-expression, whereas SSDP hardly coIPs with Pygo2 in the absence of exogenous LDB1, even at high SSDP excess (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: LDB1 overexpressed on its own is highly unstable.
source: The reverse could not be established since LDB1 overexpressed on its own is highly unstable (Figure 2D), being targeted for proteasomal degradation in the absence of SSDP (Xu et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section, demonstrated in Figure 2D, and supported by a citation.

claim: LDB1 is targeted for proteasomal degradation in the absence of SSDP.
source: The reverse could not be established since LDB1 overexpressed on its own is highly unstable (Figure 2D), being targeted for proteasomal degradation in the absence of SSDP (Xu et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation.

claim: SSDP1-92 forms a stable tetramer in solution.
source: Size exclusion chromatography coupled to multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) revealed an average apparent molecular mass of 43 kDa for the protein in this peak, which corresponds to a tetramer (expected molecular mass 42.7 kDa). Evidently, SSDP1-92 forms a stable tetramer in solution.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Chip205-436 and SSDP1-92 form a complex with a stoichiometry corresponding to an MBP-Chip dimer bound to an SSDP tetramer.
source: The peaks of these two species are not baseline-resolved during SEC-MALS, but their average masses of ∼190 kDa and ∼380 kDa suggest that the shoulder is a dimer of the major ∼190 kDa species (Figure 3B). The latter thus corresponds to an MBP-Chip dimer bound to an SSDP tetramer (expected 181 kDa), the only possible stoichiometry that fits the observed molecular mass.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The human LDB1-SSDP complex has the same architecture as the Drosophila Chip-SSDP complex.
source: The same architecture is also found for the human LDB1-SSDP complex (Figure 3C), revising previous models of ChiLS (e.g., Bronstein and Segal, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Chip-SSDP binds to wild-type but not F99A mutant Pygo67-107.
source: To monitor direct NPF-dependent binding, we incubated purified Chip-SSDP with wt and mutant 15N-labeled Lipoyl-tagged (Lip) Pygo67-107 (15N-Nterm) and recorded heteronuclear single-quantum correlation (HSQC) spectra by NMR. We thus observed clear line broadenings with wt (Figure 4A) but not with F99A mutant 15N-Nterm (bearing a point mutation in NPF; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by NMR data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: SSDP1-92 does not bind to Pygo NPF.
source: Incubation of wt 15N-Nterm with purified SSDP1-92 did not produce any spectral changes (Figure 4C), confirming that SSDP does not bind NPF (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by NMR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: LDB1-SSDP binds to wild-type but not F78A mutant Pygo2.
source: LDB1-SSDP also binds to wt but not F78A mutant Pygo2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by NMR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ChiLS 'interaction footprints' span 10 NPF-spanning residues in Pygo.
source: Assignments of double-labeled protein allowed us to determine that the ChiLS 'interaction footprints' span 10 NPF-spanning residues in Pygo, and 25 residues in Pygo2.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on NMR assignments.

claim: The ChiLS 'interaction footprints' span 25 residues in Pygo2.
source: Assignments of double-labeled protein allowed us to determine that the ChiLS 'interaction footprints' span 10 NPF-spanning residues in Pygo, and 25 residues in Pygo2.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on NMR assignments.

claim: A minimal 16-mer Pygo NPF peptide without the proline cluster produces a comparable interaction with ChiLS.
source: A minimal 16-mer without the proline cluster produces a comparable interaction (Figure 5A), showing that this cluster is dispensable in this binding assay.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The proline cluster upstream of NPF is dispensable for binding to ChiLS in NMR binding assays.
source: A minimal 16-mer without the proline cluster produces a comparable interaction (Figure 5A), showing that this cluster is dispensable in this binding assay.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The residues immediately flanking the NPF are conserved and may contribute to binding.
source: Notably, the residues immediately flanking the NPF are conserved (Figure 5A) and may contribute to binding (see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: NPF-containing fragments from MACC1, RUNX2, Runt, Lozenge, and Osa tested positive in NMR binding assays with ChiLS.
source: NPF-containing fragments from MACC1, RUNX2, Runt and Lozenge (fly RUNX proteins) and Osa tested positive in NMR binding assays, while those from ARID1B and RUNX3 were negative—somewhat curious in the latter case, given that its NPF motif resembles that of Runt (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and summarized in Figure 5A.

claim: NPF-containing fragments from ARID1B and RUNX3 tested negative in NMR binding assays with ChiLS.
source: NPF-containing fragments from MACC1, RUNX2, Runt and Lozenge (fly RUNX proteins) and Osa tested positive in NMR binding assays, while those from ARID1B and RUNX3 were negative—somewhat curious in the latter case, given that its NPF motif resembles that of Runt (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and summarized in Figure 5A.

claim: Full-length Runt coIPs efficiently with ChiLS.
source: CoIP assays revealed that full-length Runt coIPs efficiently with ChiLS (Figure 5C), more so than Pygo (Figure 5D), pointing to a second (stronger) interaction between Runt and ChiLS.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Full-length Runt coIPs with ChiLS more efficiently than Pygo.
source: CoIP assays revealed that full-length Runt coIPs efficiently with ChiLS (Figure 5C), more so than Pygo (Figure 5D), pointing to a second (stronger) interaction between Runt and ChiLS.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The N-terminal half of Runt (without NPF) coIPs with ChiLS.
source: Indeed, the N-terminal half of Runt (without NPF) coIPs with ChiLS (and vice versa), as does an NPF-mutant Runt, while the C-terminal half of Runt does not (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: An NPF-mutant Runt coIPs with ChiLS.
source: Indeed, the N-terminal half of Runt (without NPF) coIPs with ChiLS (and vice versa), as does an NPF-mutant Runt, while the C-terminal half of Runt does not (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The C-terminal half of Runt does not coIP with ChiLS.
source: Indeed, the N-terminal half of Runt (without NPF) coIPs with ChiLS (and vice versa), as does an NPF-mutant Runt, while the C-terminal half of Runt does not (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ChiLS binds directly to the Runt domain.
source: Rather, this interaction depends on the Runt domain to which ChiLS binds directly, as can be shown by NMR (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by NMR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: AML1, Runx2, and Runx3 coIP efficiently with ChiLS.
source: Efficient coIP with ChiLS was also observed for AML1, Runx2 and Runx3 (Figure 5E), consistent with the previously reported association of Runx1 with Ldb1 in differentiated mouse erythroleukemic cells (Meier et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Runx1 associates with Ldb1 in differentiated mouse erythroleukemic cells.
source: Efficient coIP with ChiLS was also observed for AML1, Runx2 and Runx3 (Figure 5E), consistent with the previously reported association of Runx1 with Ldb1 in differentiated mouse erythroleukemic cells (Meier et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation.

claim: runt is required for normal Ubx expression in the embryonic visceral mesoderm.
source: This seemed possible, given that runt is required for normal Ubx expression in the embryonic visceral mesoderm (Tremml and Bienz, 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation.

claim: runt mutant embryos lack the middle midgut constriction.
source: Staining runt mutant embryos with α-Labial antibody, we discovered that these mutants lack the middle midgut constriction, the signature phenotype found in all mutants with defective endoderm induction (including wg and pygo; Bienz, 1994; Thompson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Labial staining in runt mutant embryos is significantly weaker than in wild-type and exhibits no gradient.
source: Furthermore, staining is significantly weaker than in the wt, and exhibits no gradient (Figure 6C,D), mimicking the phenotype seen in wg mutants (Bienz, 1994; Thompson et al., 2002) (although Wg is expressed in runt mutants; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: runt is required for endoderm induction.
source: Thus, runt is required for endoderm induction, likely for the Wg response of labial.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is an inference from the phenotypic data.

claim: lab550R mediates relatively weak and even LacZ expression, limited to a narrow band of cells.
source: Similarly, lab550R mediates relatively weak and even LacZ expression, limited to a narrow band of cells (Figure 6G), which phenocopies the LacZ pattern from an enhancer with mutant dTCF binding sites (lab550L; Figure 6H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6G.

claim: lab550 is strongly activated posteriorly if Runt is expressed throughout the endoderm.
source: Importantly, lab550 is strongly activated posteriorly if Runt is expressed throughout the endoderm (Figure 6I), while neither lab500R nor lab550L are Runt-responsive (Figure 6J,K).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Neither lab500R nor lab550L are Runt-responsive.
source: Importantly, lab550 is strongly activated posteriorly if Runt is expressed throughout the endoderm (Figure 6I), while neither lab500R nor lab550L are Runt-responsive (Figure 6J,K).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6J,K.

claim: Runt acts through lab550, apparently cooperating with dTCF to render lab550 signal-responsive.
source: Thus, Runt acts through lab550, apparently cooperating with dTCF to render lab550 signal-responsive.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is an inference from the functional analysis of the lab550 enhancer.

claim: The Runt binding sites in the Ubx midgut enhancer are functional targets of Runt.
source: Likewise, the Runt binding sites in the Ubx midgut enhancer are also functional targets of Runt (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), implicating Runt in the Wg-dependent indirect autoregulation of Ubx at the top of the inductive cascade (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Runt is implicated in the Wg-dependent indirect autoregulation of Ubx at the top of the inductive cascade.
source: Likewise, the Runt binding sites in the Ubx midgut enhancer are also functional targets of Runt (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), implicating Runt in the Wg-dependent indirect autoregulation of Ubx at the top of the inductive cascade (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is an inference from the functional analysis of the Ubx enhancer.

claim: Groucho was identified as a new ChiLS-interacting factor by mass spectrometry.
source: Looking for hits with similar spectral counts in all three coIPs provided a stringent criterion that eliminated most hits (many of which were false positives as they scored highly in the Flag but not HA IPs). The resulting overlap list contains Beadex, Apterous and CG5708 as the top hits, followed by Groucho (Figure 7A), the only new hit identified with high confidence.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The WD40 domain of Groucho/TLE3 is both necessary and sufficient for association with ChiLS.
source: CoIPs confirmed the interaction between ChiLS and Groucho or TLE3, and revealed that the WD40 domain is both necessary and sufficient for association, while the Q domain and linker are dispensable (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 7B–E.

claim: The Q domain and linker of Groucho/TLE3 are dispensable for association with ChiLS.
source: CoIPs confirmed the interaction between ChiLS and Groucho or TLE3, and revealed that the WD40 domain is both necessary and sufficient for association, while the Q domain and linker are dispensable (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 7B–E.

claim: The linker of Groucho/TLE attenuates the interaction between Groucho/TLE and ChiLS.
source: Even though the minimal WD40 domain coIPs only weakly with ChiLS, the same is true for full-length Groucho, while Δlinker interacts very strongly (Figure 7C), suggesting that the linker attenuates the interaction between Groucho/Tranducin-like enhancer protein (TLE) and ChiLS, consistent with the known regulatory role of this region (controlled by phosphorylation; Turki-Judeh and Courey, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Groucho's binding to Chip neither requires its LID, nor SSDP.
source: Groucho's binding to Chip neither requires its LID, nor SSDP (M. F., unpublished).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is based on unpublished data.

claim: Groucho/TLE binds to TCF via its Q domain.
source: Crucially, since Groucho/TLE binds to TCF via its Q domain (Mieszczanek et al., 2008; Chodaparambil et al., 2014), it can thus function as an adaptor between ChiLS and TCF.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations.

claim: Groucho/TLE can function as an adaptor between ChiLS and TCF.
source: Crucially, since Groucho/TLE binds to TCF via its Q domain (Mieszczanek et al., 2008; Chodaparambil et al., 2014), it can thus function as an adaptor between ChiLS and TCF.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is an inference from the binding data.

claim: The WD40 domain of Groucho/TLE binds to the WRPY motif at the C-terminus of RUNX proteins.
source: We note that the WD40 domain also binds to the WRPY motif at the C-terminus of RUNX proteins (Canon and Banerjee, 2000; Chuang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations.

claim: chip is required for the function of remote enhancers of the homeobox genes cut and Ubx.
source: chip is required for the function of remote enhancers of the homeobox genes cut (a Notch and Wg target which patterns the wing margin), and of Ubx (Morcillo et al., 1996) which specifies the middle body region including the third leg and haltere (the dorsal appendage that substitutes for the hind wing in flies).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation.

claim: chip is required for Apterous-dependent wing development.
source: Furthermore, chip is required for Apterous-dependent wing development (Milan and Cohen, 1999), and for the notum bristles which are specified by Pannier and Achaete/Scute in a Wg-dependent fashion (Garcia–Garcia et al., 1999; Ramain et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations.

claim: chip is required for the notum bristles which are specified by Pannier and Achaete/Scute in a Wg-dependent fashion.
source: Furthermore, chip is required for Apterous-dependent wing development (Milan and Cohen, 1999), and for the notum bristles which are specified by Pannier and Achaete/Scute in a Wg-dependent fashion (Garcia–Garcia et al., 1999; Ramain et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations.

claim: ssdp mutant clones produce wing defects that phenocopy pygo mutant clones.
source: ssdp mutant clones produce wing defects that phenocopy pygo mutant clones (van Meyel et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation.

claim: The top scoring positively-regulated SSDP target genes in wing discs were linked to dTCF binding sites.
source: Strikingly, the top scoring positively-regulated SSDP target genes were linked to dTCF binding sites (although this is not mentioned in the text, but see Table S3 in Bronstein et al., 2010)—a strong indication that SSDP promotes primarily dTCF-dependent transcription in this tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation.

claim: SSDP promotes primarily dTCF-dependent transcription in wing disc tissue.
source: Strikingly, the top scoring positively-regulated SSDP target genes were linked to dTCF binding sites (although this is not mentioned in the text, but see Table S3 in Bronstein et al., 2010)—a strong indication that SSDP promotes primarily dTCF-dependent transcription in this tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is an inference from the transcriptional profiling data.

claim: chip and ssdp control dTCF targets including vestigial and wg in wing discs.
source: Clonal analysis in wing discs confirmed that chip and ssdp control dTCF targets including vestigial and wg, similarly to pygo (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: ssdp and pygo are required for high levels of Ubx expression in haltere discs.
source: In haltere discs, ssdp and pygo are required for high levels of Ubx expression, causing similar overgrowth phenotypes in halteres (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: chip has a pioneer-like role in the early embryo when zygotic transcription starts at the maternal-zygotic transition.
source: chip has a pioneer-like role in the early embryo, when zygotic transcription starts at the maternal-zygotic transition, enabling expression of segmentation genes along the antero-posterior axis (Morcillo et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation.

claim: Embryos without maternal and zygotic Chip do not develop, except for rare escapers which show severe expression defects of segmentation genes, including even-skipped.
source: We confirmed that embryos without maternal and zygotic Chip (chip germ-line clones, glcs) do not develop, except for rare escapers which show severe expression defects of segmentation genes, including even-skipped (eve) (Morcillo et al., 1997) (J. M., unpublished).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation and unpublished data.

claim: ssdp germ-line clones show only residual expression of Eve, Wg and Ubx.
source: Antibody staining of ssdp glcs revealed only residual expression of Eve, Wg and Ubx (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 8A–C.

claim: twi-LacZ appears normal in ssdp germ-line clones.
source: In contrast, twi-LacZ (recapitulating endogenous twist, a mesoderm-specifying bHLH gene activated in the ventral-most zone; Thisse et al., 1991) appears normal in ssdp glcs (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: hb-LacZ is normal in ssdp germ-line clones.
source: Likewise, hb-LacZ (recapitulating expression of endogenous hunchback, a gene specifying anterior development; Struhl et al., 1992) is normal in these mutants (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: ChiLS is required for gene activity along the antero-posterior but not the dorso-ventral axis.
source: These ssdp defects phenocopy those of chip glcs (Morcillo et al., 1997), and they indicate that ChiLS is required for gene activity along the antero-posterior but not the dorso-ventral axis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is an inference from the phenotypic data.

claim: Wg is never expressed in embryos lacking ChiLS.
source: An important corollary is that Wg is never expressed in embryos lacking ChiLS.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is an inference from the phenotypic data.

claim: The cuticles of rare chip glc escapers show a lawn of ventral denticles.
source: In support of this, the cuticles of the rare chip glc escapers show a lawn of ventral denticles (Morcillo et al., 1997), as do ssdp glcs (Figure 8F) and pygo glcs (Parker et al., 2002; Thompson et al., 2002)—the hallmark of Wg signaling failure (Cadigan and Nusse, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The cuticles of ssdp glcs show a lawn of ventral denticles.
source: In support of this, the cuticles of the rare chip glc escapers show a lawn of ventral denticles (Morcillo et al., 1997), as do ssdp glcs (Figure 8F) and pygo glcs (Parker et al., 2002; Thompson et al., 2002)—the hallmark of Wg signaling failure (Cadigan and Nusse, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The cuticles of pygo glcs show a lawn of ventral denticles.
source: In support of this, the cuticles of the rare chip glc escapers show a lawn of ventral denticles (Morcillo et al., 1997), as do ssdp glcs (Figure 8F) and pygo glcs (Parker et al., 2002; Thompson et al., 2002)—the hallmark of Wg signaling failure (Cadigan and Nusse, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations.

claim: A lawn of ventral denticles is the hallmark of Wg signaling failure.
source: In support of this, the cuticles of the rare chip glc escapers show a lawn of ventral denticles (Morcillo et al., 1997), as do ssdp glcs (Figure 8F) and pygo glcs (Parker et al., 2002; Thompson et al., 2002)—the hallmark of Wg signaling failure (Cadigan and Nusse, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation.

claim: ChiLS is the first nuclear NPF-binding factor.
source: ChiLS is the first nuclear NPF-binding factor.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: NPF binding to ChiLS appears to depend on the aromatic residue at +2, the invariant P at +1, N (or G) at 0 and NPF-adjacent residues.
source: NPF binding to ChiLS appears to depend on the same residues as NPF binding to EHD domains (de Beer et al., 2000), that is, on the aromatic residue at +2 (Figure 4), the invariant P at +1, N (or G) at 0 and NPF-adjacent residues (Figure 5A), including negative charges at +3 and +4 (whereby a positive charge at +3 abolishes binding to EHD; Kieken et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and is based on NMR data and comparison with EHD binding.

claim: Groucho/TLE is recruited to TCF via its Q domain, which tetramerizes.
source: Groucho/TLE is recruited to TCF via its Q domain, which tetramerizes (Chen et al., 1998; Chodaparambil et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: The short segment that links two Q domain dimers into a tetramer is deleted in a dTCF-specific groucho allele that abolishes dTCF binding and Wg responses.
source: Intriguingly, the short segment that links two Q domain dimers into a tetramer (Chodaparambil et al., 2014) is deleted in a dTCF-specific groucho allele that abolishes dTCF binding and Wg responses (Mieszczanek et al., 2008), suggesting that TCF may normally bind to a Groucho/TLE tetramer.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: TCF may normally bind to a Groucho/TLE tetramer.
source: Intriguingly, the short segment that links two Q domain dimers into a tetramer (Chodaparambil et al., 2014) is deleted in a dTCF-specific groucho allele that abolishes dTCF binding and Wg responses (Mieszczanek et al., 2008), suggesting that TCF may normally bind to a Groucho/TLE tetramer.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and is an inference from genetic data.

claim: Groucho/TLE uses its WD40 propeller domain to bind to other enhancer-binding proteins on Wnt-responsive enhancers.
source: Groucho/TLE uses its second domain, the WD40 propeller, to bind to other enhancer-binding proteins on Wnt-responsive enhancers (Turki-Judeh and Courey, 2012), most notably to the C-terminal WRPY motif of RUNX proteins (common partners of TCFs in Wnt-responsive enhancers; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: The WD40-dependent binding of Groucho/TLE to ChiLS can occur simultaneously with binding to the WRPY motif of RUNX proteins.
source: This interaction can occur simultaneously with the WD40-dependent binding to ChiLS (Figure 7F), given the tetramer structure of Groucho/TLE.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and is an inference from the structural data.

claim: RUNX uses its DNA-binding Runt domain to interact with HMG domains of TCFs.
source: In turn, RUNX uses its DNA-binding Runt domain to interact with HMG domains of TCFs (Kahler and Westendorf, 2003; Ito et al., 2008), and to recruit ChiLS (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: RUNX appears to be the keystone of the Wnt enhanceosome since it binds to the enhancer directly while undergoing simultaneous interactions with Groucho/TLE, TCF and ChiLS.
source: RUNX thus appears to be the keystone of the Wnt enhanceosome since it binds to the enhancer directly while undergoing simultaneous interactions with Groucho/TLE (through its C-terminal WRPY motif), TCF and ChiLS (though its Runt domain).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and is an inference from the binding data.

claim: Runt has pioneering functions in the early Drosophila embryo, shortly after the onset of zygotic transcription.
source: In line with this, Runt has pioneering functions in the early Drosophila embryo, shortly after the onset of zygotic transcription (Canon and Banerjee, 2000), and in the naïve endoderm (Figure 6) as soon as this germlayer is formed, in each case prior to the first Wg signaling events.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: Runt has pioneering functions in the naïve endoderm as soon as this germlayer is formed, prior to the first Wg signaling events.
source: In line with this, Runt has pioneering functions in the early Drosophila embryo, shortly after the onset of zygotic transcription (Canon and Banerjee, 2000), and in the naïve endoderm (Figure 6) as soon as this germlayer is formed, in each case prior to the first Wg signaling events.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: RUNX paralogs have pioneer-like functions in specifying cell lineages, including definitive hematopoiesis in flies and mammals.
source: RUNX paralogs also have pioneer-like functions in specifying cell lineages, that is, definitive hematopoiesis in flies and mammals (Chuang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: ChiLS, once tethered to the enhanceosome core complex, recruits Pygo via NPF to prime the enhancer for Wnt responses.
source: Our model predicts that ChiLS, once tethered to the enhanceosome core complex, recruits Pygo via NPF to prime the enhancer for Wnt responses (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: The binding of ChiLS to Pygo can occur simultaneously to its NPF-dependent binding to RUNX, given the dimer-tetramer architecture of ChiLS.
source: Given the dimer-tetramer architecture of ChiLS (Figure 3C), its binding to Pygo can occur simultaneously to its NPF-dependent binding to RUNX.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and is an inference from the structural data.

claim: Tethering Pygo to the Wnt enhanceosome may require Pygo's binding to methylated histone H3 tail.
source: In turn, tethering Pygo to the Wnt enhanceosome may require Pygo's binding to methylated histone H3 tail (Fiedler et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2013), similarly to Groucho/TLE whose tethering to enhancers depends on binding to hypoacetylated histone H3 and H4 tails (Sekiya and Zaret, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: Groucho/TLE tethering to enhancers depends on binding to hypoacetylated histone H3 and H4 tails.
source: In turn, tethering Pygo to the Wnt enhanceosome may require Pygo's binding to methylated histone H3 tail (Fiedler et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2013), similarly to Groucho/TLE whose tethering to enhancers depends on binding to hypoacetylated histone H3 and H4 tails (Sekiya and Zaret, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: Pygo's histone binding requires at least one methyl group at K4, the hallmark of poised enhancers.
source: Interestingly, Pygo's histone binding requires at least one methyl group at K4 (Fiedler et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2013)—the hallmark of poised enhancers (Kharchenko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: Drosophila Pygo recognizes asymmetrically di-methylated arginine 2, a hallmark of silent chromatin.
source: Indeed, Drosophila Pygo is highly unorthodox due to an architectural change in its histone-binding surface that allows it to recognize asymmetrically di-methylated arginine 2 (Miller et al., 2013)—a hallmark of silent chromatin (Kirmizis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: Unorthodox Pygo proteins may recognize silent enhancers even earlier, long before their activation.
source: Thus, the rare unorthodox Pygo proteins (Miller et al., 2013) may recognize silent enhancers even earlier, long before their activation, consistent with the early embryonic function of Pygo, prior to Wg signaling (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and is an inference from the histone binding data and embryonic phenotypes.

claim: Overcoming the OFF state imposed on the enhancer by Groucho/TLE involves Pygo-dependent capturing of β-catenin/Armadillo.
source: Overcoming the OFF state imposed on the enhancer by Groucho/TLE (Mieszczanek et al., 2008) involves Pygo-dependent capturing of β-catenin/Armadillo, which recruits various transcriptional co-activators to its C-terminus (Mosimann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: β-catenin/Armadillo recruits various transcriptional co-activators to its C-terminus.
source: Overcoming the OFF state imposed on the enhancer by Groucho/TLE (Mieszczanek et al., 2008) involves Pygo-dependent capturing of β-catenin/Armadillo, which recruits various transcriptional co-activators to its C-terminus (Mosimann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: CBP tethering to TCF enhancers is likely to co-depend on CRE-binding factors (CREB, c-Fos) and SMAD which synergize with Armadillo to activate these enhancers.
source: Although these include CREB-binding protein (CBP), a histone acetyl transferase, its tethering to TCF enhancers is likely to co-depend on CRE-binding factors (CREB, c-Fos) and SMAD (Bienz, 1997; Waltzer and Bienz, 1999) which synergize with Armadillo to activate these enhancers (Bienz, 1997; Waltzer and Bienz, 1999)—similarly to the interferon-β enhanceosome where CBP recruitment also co-depends on multiple enhancer-binding proteins (Panne et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: Acetylation of the Wnt enhancer chromatin could promote the eviction of Groucho/TLE.
source: The ensuing acetylation of the Wnt enhancer chromatin could promote the eviction of Groucho/TLE whose chromatin anchoring is blocked by acetylation of histone H3 and H4 tails (Chodaparambil et al., 2014), thus initiating the ON state.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: Groucho/TLE chromatin anchoring is blocked by acetylation of histone H3 and H4 tails.
source: The ensuing acetylation of the Wnt enhancer chromatin could promote the eviction of Groucho/TLE whose chromatin anchoring is blocked by acetylation of histone H3 and H4 tails (Chodaparambil et al., 2014), thus initiating the ON state.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: Osa antagonizes Wg responses throughout development.
source: Osa antagonizes Wg responses throughout development, and represses UbxB through its CRE (Collins and Treisman, 2000), which also mediates repression in response to high Wg signaling (Yu et al., 1998) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: Osa represses UbxB through its CRE.
source: Osa antagonizes Wg responses throughout development, and represses UbxB through its CRE (Collins and Treisman, 2000), which also mediates repression in response to high Wg signaling (Yu et al., 1998) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: Osa could terminate enhancer activity by displacing HAT-recruiting enhancer-binding proteins such as CREB and c-Fos from CREs.
source: Osa could therefore terminate enhancer activity, by displacing HAT-recruiting enhancer-binding proteins such as CREB and c-Fos from CREs and by cooperating with repressive enhancer-binding proteins such as Brinker (a Groucho-recruiting repressor that displaces SMAD from UbxB; Saller and Bienz, 2001; Saller et al., 2002) to re-recruit Groucho/TLE to the enhancer, thereby re-establishing its OFF state (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and is an inference from the known functions of Osa.

claim: Osa binds Chip to repress various Wg and ChiLS targets including achaete-scute and dLMO.
source: Notably, Osa binds Chip, to repress various Wg and ChiLS targets including achaete-scute and dLMO (Heitzler et al., 2003; Milan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: ChiLS is a coincidence detector of multiple enhancer-binding proteins and NPF proteins.
source: Therefore, ChiLS is not only a coincidence detector of multiple enhancer-binding proteins and NPF proteins, but also a switch module that exchanges positively- and negatively-acting enhancer-binding proteins (through LID) and NPF factors, to confer signal-induced activation, or re-repression (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and is an inference from the binding data and functional analysis.

claim: ChiLS is a switch module that exchanges positively- and negatively-acting enhancer-binding proteins and NPF factors.
source: Therefore, ChiLS is not only a coincidence detector of multiple enhancer-binding proteins and NPF proteins, but also a switch module that exchanges positively- and negatively-acting enhancer-binding proteins (through LID) and NPF factors, to confer signal-induced activation, or re-repression (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and is an inference from the binding data and functional analysis.

claim: The stoichiometry and modularity of ChiLS renders it ideally suited to function as a coincidence detector and switch module.
source: Its stoichiometry and modularity renders it ideally suited to both tasks.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and is an inference from the structural data.

claim: The interferon-β enhanceosome does not contain a similar integrating module to ChiLS.
source: We note that the interferon-β enhanceosome does not contain a similar integrating module (Panne et al., 2007), perhaps because it is dedicated to a single signaling input.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: ChiLS is essential for activation of master-regulatory genes in the early embryo.
source: ChiLS is essential for activation of master-regulatory genes in the early embryo (Morcillo et al., 1997) (Figure 8), similarly to DNA-binding pioneer factors such as Zelda (in the Drosophila embryo) or FoxA (in the mammalian endoderm) which render enhancers accessible to enhancer-binding proteins (Zaret and Carroll, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations and supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: ChiLS maintains HOX gene expression throughout development.
source: Moreover, ChiLS maintains HOX gene expression throughout development (Figure 5; Figure 8—figure supplement 2), enabling Wg to sustain HOX autoregulation, a mechanism commonly observed to ensure coordinate expression of HOX genes in groups of cells (Bienz, 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation and supported by data in Figure 5 and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Chip is thought to facilitate enhancer-promoter communication.
source: Another hallmark of pioneer factors is that they initiate communication with the basal transcription machinery associated with the promoter. Chip is thought to facilitate enhancer-promoter communication (Morcillo et al., 1997), possibly by bridging enhancers and promoters through self-association (Cross et al., 2010) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: Ldb1 occupies both remote enhancers and transcription start sites.
source: Indeed, Ldb1 occupies both remote enhancers and transcription start sites (e.g., of globin genes and c-Myb; Love et al., 2014), likely looping enhancers to the basal transcription machinery at promoters (Deng et al., 2012; Stadhouders et al., 2012) which requires self-association (Krivega et al., 2014), but possibly also other factors (such as cohesin, or mediator; Levine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: Ldb1 likely loops enhancers to the basal transcription machinery at promoters.
source: Indeed, Ldb1 occupies both remote enhancers and transcription start sites (e.g., of globin genes and c-Myb; Love et al., 2014), likely looping enhancers to the basal transcription machinery at promoters (Deng et al., 2012; Stadhouders et al., 2012) which requires self-association (Krivega et al., 2014), but possibly also other factors (such as cohesin, or mediator; Levine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: Enhancer-promoter looping by Ldb1 requires self-association.
source: Indeed, Ldb1 occupies both remote enhancers and transcription start sites (e.g., of globin genes and c-Myb; Love et al., 2014), likely looping enhancers to the basal transcription machinery at promoters (Deng et al., 2012; Stadhouders et al., 2012) which requires self-association (Krivega et al., 2014), but possibly also other factors (such as cohesin, or mediator; Levine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: chip has been linked predominantly to Notch-regulated processes in Drosophila.
source: Previous genetic analysis in Drosophila has linked chip predominantly to Notch-regulated processes (Bronstein and Segal, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: groucho was initially thought to be dedicated to repression downstream of Notch.
source: Likewise, groucho was initially thought to be dedicated to repression downstream of Notch (Preiss et al., 1988), before its role in antagonizing TCF and Wnt responses emerged (Roose and Clevers, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: Lozenge facilitates Notch responses in the developing eye and in hematocytes.
source: Moreover, Lozenge facilitates Notch responses in the developing eye, and in hematocytes (Canon and Banerjee, 2000; Terriente-Felix et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: Mouse Ldb1 has been implicated in Wnt-related processes, based on phenotypic analysis of Ldb1 knock-out embryos and tissues.
source: Indeed, mouse Ldb1 has been implicated in Wnt-related processes, based on phenotypic analysis of Ldb1 knock-out embryos and tissues (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2003; Mylona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: Ldb1 has wide-spread roles in various murine stem cell compartments that are controlled by Wnt signaling.
source: Notably, Ldb1 has wide-spread roles in various murine stem cell compartments that are controlled by Wnt signaling (Xu et al., 2007a; Dey-Guha et al., 2009; Li et al., 2011; Salmans et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: The Wnt enhanceosome may be switchable to Notch-responsive by NPF factor exchange and/or LMO-mediated enhancer-binding protein exchange at ChiLS.
source: An interesting corollary is that the Wnt enhanceosome may be switchable to Notch-responsive, by NPF factor exchange and/or LMO-mediated enhancer-binding protein exchange at ChiLS (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and is an inference from the binding data and known functions of ChiLS components.

claim: HES repressors are universally induced by Notch signaling and bind to ChiLS enhancers to re-recruit Groucho/TLE via their WRPW motifs.
source: Hairy/Enhancer-of-split (HES) repressors could be pivotal for this switch (Delidakis et al., 2014): these bHLH factors are universally induced by Notch signaling, and they bind to ChiLS enhancers to re-recruit Groucho/TLE via their WRPW motifs (Turki-Judeh and Courey, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: HES repressors may be capable of re-establishing the OFF state on Wnt enhancers in response to Notch.
source: HES repressors may thus be capable of re-establishing the OFF state on Wnt enhancers in response to Notch.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and is an inference from the known functions of HES repressors.

claim: Restoring a high histone-binding affinity in Drosophila Pygo by reversing the architectural change in its histone-binding surface towards human renders it hyperactive towards both Wg and Notch targets.
source: Notably, restoring a high histone-binding affinity in Drosophila Pygo by reversing the architectural change in its histone-binding surface towards human renders it hyperactive towards both Wg and Notch targets (Miller et al., 2013) even though pygo is not normally required for Notch responses in flies.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: pygo is not normally required for Notch responses in flies.
source: Notably, restoring a high histone-binding affinity in Drosophila Pygo by reversing the architectural change in its histone-binding surface towards human renders it hyperactive towards both Wg and Notch targets (Miller et al., 2013) even though pygo is not normally required for Notch responses in flies.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: Humanized Pygo may resist the Notch-mediated shut-down of the Wnt enhanceosome, owing to its elevated histone affinity that boosts its enhancer tethering.
source: Humanized Pygo may thus resist the Notch-mediated shut-down of the Wnt enhanceosome, owing to its elevated histone affinity that boosts its enhancer tethering, which could delay its eviction from the enhanceosome by repressive NPF factors.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and is an inference from the histone binding data.

claim: Orthodox Pygo proteins (as found in most animals and humans) confer both Wnt and Notch responses.
source: The apparent Notch-responsiveness of the Wnt enhanceosome supports our notion that orthodox Pygo proteins (as found in most animals and humans) confer both Wnt and Notch responses (Miller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: The components of the Wnt enhanceosome have pivotal roles in stem cell compartments.
source: Previous genetic studies have shown that the components of the Wnt enhanceosome (e.g., TCF, RUNX, ChiLS and LHX) have pivotal roles in stem cell compartments, as already mentioned (see also Folgueras et al., 2013; Lien and Fuchs, 2014), suggesting a universal function of this enhanceosome in stem cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: Dysregulation of the Wnt enhanceosome by hyperactive β-catenin is a root cause of cancer, most notably colorectal cancer but also other epithelial cancers.
source: It is therefore hardly surprising that its dysregulation, that is, by hyperactive β-catenin, is a root cause of cancer, most notably colorectal cancer but also other epithelial cancers (Clevers, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: AML1 and RUNX3 are tumour suppressors whose inactivation is prevalent in myeloid and lymphocytic leukemias and in a wide range of solid tumors including colorectal cancer.
source: Indeed, genetic evidence implicates almost every one of its components (as inferred from the fly counterparts) in cancer: AML1 and RUNX3 are tumour suppressors whose inactivation is prevalent in myeloid and lymphocytic leukemias (Mangan and Speck, 2011), and in a wide range of solid tumors including colorectal cancer (Chuang et al., 2013), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: ARID1A is a wide-spread tumor suppressor frequently inactivated in various epithelial cancers.
source: Likewise, ARID1A is a wide-spread tumor suppressor frequently inactivated in various epithelial cancers (Wu and Roberts, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: Many T-cell acute leukemias can be attributed to inappropriate expression of LMO2.
source: Furthermore, many T-cell acute leukemias can be attributed to inappropriate expression of LMO2 (Rabbitts, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: AML1 and ARID1A behave as haplo-insufficient tumor suppressors.
source: Intriguingly, AML1 and ARID1A behave as haplo-insufficient tumor suppressors, consistent with the notion that these factors compete with activating NPF factors such as Pygo2, RUNX2 and possibly MACC1 (predictive of metastatic colorectal cancer; Stein et al., 2009) for binding to ChiLS, which will be interesting to test in future.

claim: MACC1 is predictive of metastatic colorectal cancer.
